title: The monkey gardeners
hook: monkeys water the saplings by pulling each one up to check its roots (Jataka 46)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the baka, the crane, and the crab: a sweet promise, a pile of bones, and a crab who held on. Your line was the crab remembers. Did you keep a claw on one offer? Today, helpers who mean well, and ruin everything. Day eight hundred twenty-five.

There's a festival in the city of Benares, crowds and celebration in every street, and the king's gardener badly wants to go. But the young trees in the royal park need water while he's away. Then he has an idea. A troop of monkeys lives in the park. They eat the fruit, they enjoy the shade; surely they owe him a favor. He goes to their king and asks. The monkey king says: of course. Leave it to us.
screen: `A FESTIVAL IN THE CITY.` → `THE SAPLINGS NEED WATER.` → `LEAVE IT TO US.`

segments.voice: First, the job. The gardener hands over the water skins and the wooden pots and goes off to the festival. The monkey king gathers his troop and gives the order to water the young trees. Second, the plan. But water is precious, the monkey king tells them. We mustn't waste it. So before you water a tree, pull it up and look at its roots. Trees with long roots get a lot. Trees with short roots get a little. It's careful. It's thrifty. It sounds like good management. Third, the result. So the monkeys go through the park, tree by tree, pulling each sapling out of the ground, inspecting the roots, and watering accordingly. And every young tree they check, they kill. Fourth, the witness. A wise man walking through the park, the bodhisatta in this tale, sees the monkeys at work and asks what they're doing. They explain: their king's orders. And he says, in a verse, that the ignorant, trying to do good, do harm instead, like the monkeys in the king's garden. What makes the tale sharp is that nobody is wicked. The monkeys aren't lazy, and they aren't greedy. They're conscientious. They wanted to be sure. And being sure, here, meant digging up the very thing that needed to stay hidden in the dark to grow. A root does its work out of sight.
screen: `THE GARDENER GOES TO THE FESTIVAL.` · `CHECK THE ROOTS, SAVE THE WATER.` · `EVERY TREE THEY CHECK DIES.` · `HARM FROM TRYING TO HELP.` · then, large: `DON'T PULL UP THE ROOTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one thing grow unchecked. Bring to mind something young in your life. A plan, a relationship, a habit, a skill, someone you're helping along. Notice if you've been pulling it up to look at its roots. Checking it, measuring it, asking if it's working yet. Now picture setting it back in the ground and patting the soil down. Water it, and leave it alone. Breathe, and let it be underground for a while. The bell holds the time.
Conscientious. What the monkey gardeners were, careful helpers who pulled up every sapling to measure its roots, and killed what they meant to save. Today's word.
Your line: don't pull up the roots. Today, catch yourself once checking on something that needs time, and leave it in the ground instead. Day eight hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the Aramadusaka Jataka as a lesson that good intentions need wisdom too, and that checking too soon can do harm.

what it means: careful helpers kill the young trees by pulling them up to check their roots.
what a scholar hears: the bodhisatta's verse says the ignorant, trying to do good, do harm; good intention without wisdom is the warning.
